$doc: Vyomi capability registry — Azure Virtual machines. See aws/s3.json for the contract.

azure.vms.vm.crud.title: Virtual machines (create, get, list, delete) over ARM

azure.vms.power.title: Start, restart, stop (power off) and delete
limitations: Power actions update the virtual machine's logical power state (properties.powerState) only — there is no LXD/container runtime backing a virtual machine in-browser, so nothing is actually booted or halted. Hibernate and Capture are not modelled.

azure.vms.size.title: Size (list sizes, resize)
limitations: The size list is a curated sample of real Azure VM size names and vCPU/RAM (core/instance_catalog.py) served over GET .../virtualMachines/{vm}/vmSizes, not the full regional catalog. Series and Max IOPS are derived server-side from each size's vCPU count/family rather than Azure's published per-SKU specs, and Cost/month is a rough estimate derived from vCPU/RAM rather than live Azure retail pricing.

azure.vms.disks.title: Disks (OS disk, data disks)
limitations: Standalone managed disks (Microsoft.Compute/disks, core/azure_disks_core.py) are real ARM resources: SKU / createOption (Empty needs a size, Copy/Restore need an existing source) / size 1..32767 validated, grow-only, derived diskState + managedBy + SKU-tier IOPS/MBps. Attach existing disks lists unattached disks in the VM region; attaching validates existence, region, unique LUN and that the disk is not attached to another VM (409 DiskAlreadyAttached); an attached disk cannot be deleted or have its SKU changed, growing it needs the VM deallocated, and deleting a VM detaches (keeps) its disks. Disk contents are never exposed to a guest; encryption sets, shared disks and snapshots-as-resources are not modelled.

The OS disk and 'Create and attach a new disk' data disks are embedded on the virtual machine (properties.storageProfile), the shape the create wizard writes; only disks attached from the standalone resources below are linked to a Microsoft.Compute/disks record. Detaching a data disk is real.

azure.vms.networking.title: Networking (network interface, public IP, inbound/outbound port rules)
limitations: The virtual machine's network interface (Microsoft.Network/networkInterfaces), its public IP address (Microsoft.Network/publicIPAddresses, when requested at create time — the create wizard's 'Public IP' field is real, not a stub) and, when a network security group is attached, its inbound/outbound rules (Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups/securityRules) are real ARM resources and real CRUD — the same engine the Network security groups console uses. Load balancing, Application security groups and Network manager are an honest gap (this lens does not model those resource types), and attaching a public IP to an EXISTING virtual machine after creation is not modelled (real Azure itself requires a NIC swap for that).

azure.vms.connect.title: Connect (SSH command)
limitations: The displayed SSH command is built from the virtual machine's real admin username and its public IP address when one was requested at create time (else its network interface's private IP address), and on the offline appliance (Docker-backed VM) it is a real sshd login with the shared key. Serial console (GET /api/azure/vm/{id}/serial-console) returns the guest's real dmesg/process view and a line-at-a-time docker-exec shell (not a UART); Bastion Connect (POST /api/azure/vm/{id}/bastion/connect) opens a browser-shell session record plus the ssh command, with no Bastion host, subnet or NSG data plane (that stays under networking). On Nano (in-browser VMs turned on) the VM is a real Linux VM inside the browser tab (v86, 32-bit x86 Alpine, not the marketplace image): Connect and Serial console show its boot state, an xterm.js shell on the VM serial console (root, no tunnel needed) and an ssh command that works only through the local vyomi-tunnel (>= 1.1.0) while the tab is open. Nano limits: 32-bit x86 only; the VM's RAM is its disk (Stop saves it, Delete discards it); a background tab runs the VM several times slower; no general internet egress (only plain-HTTP URLs that allow CORS); the 21 MB image and 2 MB engine load on first launch only; with in-browser VMs off Connect offers a Turn on in-browser VMs button. Bastion and the docker-exec serial view are offline-only.

azure.vms.identity.title: Identity (system-assigned managed identity)
limitations: Lifted off config_only (wave 5b): turning identity.type to SystemAssigned really mints a stable principalId/tenantId (core/azure_arm_core._vm_identity_view), not a client-invented value, and clears them again when turned back off. The identity is genuinely HONOURED by another resource's real access check: Run command's simulated IMDS endpoint mints this identity's own token, and using that token to fetch a Key Vault secret is checked for real against the Key Vault's own Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments (core/azure_arm_core.AzureArm._check_access) — a role assignment that does not grant secrets/get is really denied, one that does is really allowed. There is no live IMDS network endpoint a process inside the VM could call on its own (no guest OS process exists in-browser) — the token can only be minted through Run command's own script interpreter, and only the Key Vault data plane consults it (no other resource's access checks honour it yet).

azure.vms.auto_shutdown.title: Auto-shutdown schedule
limitations: ENFORCED lazily: Vyomi has no real background scheduler, but once the configured local time (any Azure-style '(UTC±HH:MM) …' zone, or plain 'UTC') has passed today, the virtual machine's own power state really does flip to stopped the next time it is read (console load, GET, or list) — not necessarily at the exact minute if nothing reads it sooner. A manual Start after that sticks for the rest of the calendar day. The notification settings (time zone label aside) round-trip as configured but are not acted on — Vyomi never sends the pre-shutdown notification email or webhook.

azure.vms.locks.title: Resource locks (Microsoft.Authorization/locks), scoped to this virtual machine

azure.vms.activity_log.title: Activity log
limitations: Only console/SDK-triggered mutations made since the simulation booted are recorded (no historical backfill). The timespan picker is ENFORCED (narrowing it to e.g. 'Last hour' really drops older events via eventTimestamp ge on the query), but severity/category filtering is not modelled, and `caller` is a fixed placeholder identity rather than the real signed-in principal.

azure.vms.export_template.title: Export template (ARM/Bicep/Terraform generated client-side from this resource)
limitations: Download, Add to library, Deploy and Visualize template are honest 'Not simulated' actions — only template generation from the virtual machine's current ARM properties is real.

azure.vms.iam.title: Access control (IAM): role assignments and built-in role definitions over ARM
limitations: Role assignments and role definitions are real ARM resources (Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments, roleDefinitions). The Role assignments list is ENFORCED scoped to this virtual machine (plus its subscription/resource-group ancestors, matching real Azure's inherited-access view) instead of the whole subscription — the same engine the Cosmos DB account blade uses; Roles stays subscription-wide, which matches real Azure (built-in role definitions are listed tenant-wide too). Assignments are still created at the subscription scope (az role assignment create), and 'Check access' / 'My access' evaluation and Deny assignments / Classic administrators remain an honest gap. Update: the Deny assignments list, Classic administrators (a read-only list of the subscription's account administrator, like the real API) and My access (the simulated signed-in principal, evaluated with checkAccess) are now real shared tabs (azure.common.*); the gap wording above predates them.

azure.vms.run_command.title: Run command
limitations: Lifted off not_simulated (wave 5b): a browser/WASM simulator cannot spawn a separate guest OS process to run an arbitrary script in, so this is a bounded, deterministic interpreter (core/azure_arm_core.AzureArm._vm_run_command) rather than a general-purpose shell — it recognizes a small fixed set of whole-script shapes end to end and runs each one for REAL against this VM's own data: echo/Write-Output/Write-Host, hostname (the VM's real computer name), whoami (its real admin username), date/Get-Date, uname, and the IMDS-token-then-Key-Vault-secret-fetch pattern (169.254.169.254 oauth2/token, then https://<vault>.vault.azure.net/secrets/<name>) that exercises azure.vms.identity's real RBAC enforcement end to end. The VM must be running (a real 409, same guard start/stop uses). Any other script fails honestly with a non-zero exit and an explanatory message — never a fabricated success.

azure.vms.monitoring.title: Insights, Alerts, Metrics, Diagnostic settings, Logs, Connection monitor, Workbooks
limitations: Lifted off not_simulated (wave 5b) by wiring each tab to the SAME generic engine another lens resource already uses for real, scoped to this virtual machine — never a second, parallel implementation: Diagnostic settings is the generic Microsoft.Insights/diagnosticSettings ARM extension resource every lens resource can use (core/azure_arm_core.AzureArm._diagnostic_settings, same as the ACR/APIM blades); Alerts creates/lists real Microsoft.Insights/metricAlerts + activityLogAlerts scoped to this VM's id (core/azure_monitor_core.py, same engine the Monitor service's own Alert rules page uses); Workbooks is the same real Microsoft.Insights/workbooks gallery, sourceId = this VM; Logs runs a real bounded KQL query (core/azure_operationalinsights_core.py) against the AzureActivity table pre-filtered to this VM's own real Activity log rows; Connection monitor reuses the shared netsim evaluator (core/azure_arm_core.AzureArm._nw_connectivity_check) so a reachability check is decided by this VM's actual attached network security group rules, exactly like the Network security groups / Virtual networks consoles' own connectivity-check tool; Insights shows this VM's own real inventory/properties (the azure.monitor.resource_insights pattern). Metrics' scope/resource picker is real; the chart plots only the one metric every resource has (Activity operations, a count of this VM's own Activity log rows, as in azure.monitor.metrics_charts) — there is no Percentage CPU / network series because the VM's guest is not metered into Azure Monitor.

azure.vms.resource_visualizer.title: Resource visualizer
limitations: A real diagram of this VM's own currently-attached ARM relationships (network interface, public IP, network security group, OS/data disks) — not a generated topology layout, just this VM's real data rendered as nodes/edges.

azure.vms.advisor.title: Advisor recommendations
limitations: Recommendations are derived from this VM's own real configuration (auto-shutdown off, identity off, no restore points, Defender findings) — not Azure Advisor's own broader usage-pattern/cost heuristics, same style of simplification as azure.monitor.advisor_recommendations.

azure.vms.diagnose.title: Diagnose and solve problems
limitations: Checks this VM's own real power state, disk-encryption posture (reusing the Microsoft Defender for Cloud rule engine's finding) and whether a network interface is attached — not Azure's much larger guided-troubleshooting catalog (boot failures, RDP/SSH connectivity probes into the guest), which needs a live guest OS/hypervisor this lens does not run.

azure.vms.resource_health.title: Resource health
limitations: Derived from this VM's own real power state and lock state; there is no hypervisor health telemetry (platform events, host maintenance) to roll up in a browser/WASM simulator.

azure.vms.change_tracking.title: Change tracking
limitations: A filtered view of this VM's own real Activity log (write/extension/redeploy/reapply/reset-password operations) — not file- or registry-level change tracking inside the guest, which needs a live guest OS agent this lens does not run.

azure.vms.defender.title: Microsoft Defender for Cloud
limitations: Real findings scoped to this VM's own resource id over the SAME foundational CSPM rule engine the Defender for Cloud service's own Recommendations page uses (core/azure_security_core.py) — currently only the VM-attached encryption-at-host/disk-encryption rule; a finding attached to this VM's network security group (management ports open to the internet) surfaces on the Network security groups console's own Defender view instead, matching how this engine scopes findings to the resource they are attached to. Runtime threat alerts are not simulated (Vyomi runs no workload telemetry).

azure.vms.backup.title: Backup
limitations: "Backup as a snapshot": create/list/delete a real restore point (Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/{vm}/providers/Microsoft.Compute/restorePoints) that captures this VM's own ARM properties document, and restore really overwrites the VM's current properties with the captured ones (core/azure_arm_core.AzureArm._vm_backup) — not a standalone Recovery Services vault/backup policy schedule, which this lens does not model.

azure.vms.inventory_os.title: Operating system, Inventory
limitations: Shows this VM's own real OS type/computer name/image reference (ARM properties already stored, not fabricated) — not an installed-software/package inventory, which needs a guest-OS scanning agent and no guest OS process runs in a browser/WASM simulator.

azure.vms.configuration.title: Configuration
limitations: The boot diagnostics toggle really PATCHes this VM's own properties.diagnosticsProfile (the same generic ARM PATCH every other settings tab on this blade uses) — enabling it does not start a hypervisor serial/screenshot capture stream (azure.vms.tools' Boot diagnostics page), since no hypervisor exists in a browser/WASM simulator. VM agent / other guest-level configuration toggles are not modelled.

azure.vms.availability_scaling.title: Availability + scaling
limitations: Shows this VM's own real availability zone (properties.zones, when requested at create time) and the correctly-derived 'no infrastructure redundancy required' default; Virtual Machine Scale Set membership and flexible-orchestration scale-out are not modelled (this lens does not simulate a second host to spread instances across).

azure.vms.tools.title: Diagnose and solve problems, Resource visualizer, Bastion, Load balancing, Application security groups, Network manager, Extensions + applications, Operating system, Configuration, Advisor recommendations, Availability + scaling, Microsoft Defender for Cloud, Backup, Disaster recovery, Updates, Inventory, Change tracking, Tasks, Resource health, Boot diagnostics, Performance diagnostics, Reset password, Redeploy + reapply, Serial console, Support + Troubleshooting
limitations: Lifted off not_simulated (wave 5b) for most of this bucket — each now has its own capability id with a real backend behind it: Diagnose and solve problems (azure.vms.diagnose), Resource visualizer (azure.vms.resource_visualizer), Advisor recommendations (azure.vms.advisor), Resource health (azure.vms.resource_health), Change tracking (azure.vms.change_tracking), Microsoft Defender for Cloud (azure.vms.defender), Backup (azure.vms.backup), Operating system / Inventory (azure.vms.inventory_os), Configuration (azure.vms.configuration), Availability + scaling (azure.vms.availability_scaling). Reset password and Redeploy + reapply are real POST actions handled directly by this id — core/azure_arm_core.AzureArm._arm_action's resetPassword verb really overwrites the VM's osProfile admin username/password (reflected immediately in Connect's SSH command), and redeploy/reapply really flip the VM's power state and stamp a real instanceView timestamp.

Still honestly not simulated, for a concrete physical reason rather than 'not modelled': Bastion (no virtual network stack in a browser/WASM simulator to carry a tunnel between two simulated VMs; Load balancing now has its own capability id, azure.vms.loadbalancing), Application security groups and Network manager (same missing packet path, plus unmodelled resource types), Extensions + applications (installing an extension means a real guest agent executing a package inside a guest OS — no guest OS process runs in-browser), Updates and Performance diagnostics (need a live guest OS process to scan/sample — none runs in-browser), Boot diagnostics and Serial console (need a hypervisor video/console device to capture from or attach to — none exists in a browser/WASM simulator), Tasks (Microsoft To Do/Planner over Microsoft Graph — a real separate Microsoft 365 product), Support + Troubleshooting (files/reads a ticket against Microsoft's own real support system — a real third-party service).

azure.vms.loadbalancing.title: Load balancing (Microsoft.Network/loadBalancers + VM network-interface backend pool membership)
limitations: Real Microsoft.Network/loadBalancers (core/azure_lb_core.py): frontend IP configurations (the public IP must exist and match the SKU, or a subnet must exist), backend pools, Tcp/Http/Https probes, load-balancing rules (frontend/pool/probe must exist in the same load balancer, port and idle-timeout ranges, unique frontend port per frontend, HA ports, Standard rules need a probe), inbound NAT rules and Standard-only outbound rules, with derived child ids. A VM joins a pool through its network interface ipConfiguration (the pool must exist; the load balancer lists it as a backendIPConfiguration, and a load balancer that still has members cannot be deleted). NO traffic is balanced and NO health-probe packet is sent: the backend state shown is derived only from the VM's power state (VM running (probe not executed) / not running), never a fabricated Up/Down. Global-tier cross-region frontends are validated configuration only.

azure.vms.asgs.title: Application security groups (VM network interface membership)
limitations: Real Microsoft.Network/applicationSecurityGroups; a VM joins them through its NIC ip configuration (up to 20, each must exist and be in the NIC's region); NSG rules may name groups as source/destination (cannot combine with a non-* prefix) and a group in use cannot be deleted. Rules naming groups are evaluated by the netsim engine; the offline iptables path (LXD-era) does not resolve groups.

azure.vms.backup.title: Azure Backup for VMs (Recovery Services vault, policies, recovery points, restore)
limitations: Backup policies' schedulePolicy (Daily/Weekly run time, Hourly interval) really run from the shared scheduler tick (core/schedule_core): a protected item gets a recovery point on schedule and recovery points past retention are removed unless the vault is Locked. Offline: background loop; Nano: only while the page is open; missed runs coalesce into one.

Real: vault/policy validation, protected items, on-demand backup writes a JSON recovery-point artifact into the simulator's Blob store (account vyomirsvault), restore as restore-disks, new VM (alternate location) or original-location config reset, jobs, soft delete, immutability.

Recovery points capture the VM configuration and disk metadata, not block-level disk bytes; a restored VM boots from its configuration. Scheduled backups follow the policy (see above). Cross-region restore uses records in the single data plane.

azure.vms.disaster_recovery.title: Site Recovery: VM replication, test failover, failover, re-protect
limitations: Real: enable replication to another region/resource group (validated), test failover/unplanned failover create a replica VM + NIC in the target virtual network from the replicated configuration, cleanup, commit, re-protect, replication jobs.
Replication is snapshot-based in one data plane: RPO is always 0 and replication health Normal; no disk data is streamed; the target region is a label.

azure.vms.boot_diagnostics.title: Boot diagnostics (serial log + screenshot)
limitations: POST .../retrieveBootDiagnosticsData is real ARM (400 BootDiagnosticsNotEnabled until diagnosticsProfile.bootDiagnostics.enabled, SAS expiry validated) and writes the serial log and screenshot as blobs in the vyomibootdiag account. On the offline appliance the page also shows the guest container's real dmesg (GET /api/azure/vm/{id}/serial-console); on Nano, and wherever the host injects no guest log, the serial blob holds Vyomi's own lifecycle record and says so. The screenshot is ALWAYS a blank placeholder PNG: Vyomi has no virtual display adapter to capture.

azure.vms.serial_console_bastion.title: Serial console and Bastion connect
limitations: Offline appliance: the Serial console page and the Bastion connect page drive the guest container through the existing docker-exec routes (GET /api/azure/vm/{id}/serial-console, POST /api/azure/vm/{id}/bastion/connect, core/ssh_access_core.py), a line-at-a-time shell, not a UART or an HTTPS tunnel. Bastion needs a real Bastion host (AzureBastionSubnet) in the VM's virtual network, otherwise the page says so. Nano has no guest runtime or inbound TCP, so both pages show that honestly instead of a terminal.

azure.vms.extensions.title: Extensions + applications (Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/extensions)
limitations: Extensions are real ARM child resources of the VM (create, list, get, delete with publisher/type/typeHandlerVersion/settings), listed and installed from the console; the extension package is not downloaded and its code is not run inside a guest, so provisioningState is Succeeded without a guest agent. VM applications (gallery applications) are not modelled.

azure.vms.guest_views.title: Inventory, Update Manager and Performance diagnostics read from the running guest
limitations: Offline appliance: scripts run in the VM's real container via docker exec (GET /api/azure/vm/{id}/guest/inventory|performance|updates, POST .../updates to refresh the package index or install pending updates): the installed packages come from dpkg/apk/rpm, counters from /proc, pending updates from apt/apk against the guest's own index. Installing updates needs the container to have network access to its mirrors. Windows guests, Update Manager schedules/maintenance configurations and per-update classification (security/critical) are not modelled. Nano has no guest runtime on these pages (the v86 shell is separate), so they say so instead of inventing data.
